I enjoy building and testing hardware because it forces me to connect classroom fundamentals with real engineering constraints. My main interest is aerospace thermal systems, especially thermal protection and thermal control, where heat transfer, materials, fluids, manufacturing, and testing all come together. I am interested in work that requires first-principles thinking, hands-on iteration, and designing hardware that can survive extreme environments.

Technical Skills Snapshot

What I bring to a thermal hardware team

My foundation comes from coursework in thermodynamics, heat transfer, fluid mechanics, and combustion, and I have applied those fundamentals through rocket engine cooling, spacecraft fire safety research, FDM thermal protection testing, and Mars rover thermal control design.

Thermodynamics Heat Transfer Fluid Mechanics Combustion Composite Materials Controls Manufacturing

Thermal-Fluid Fundamentals

Applied conduction, convection, radiation, thermal resistance networks, Biot number checks, transient heating, and energy balances to real hardware and test data.

Regenerative Cooling Design

Sized cooling-channel geometry using hydraulic diameter, Reynolds number, Dittus-Boelter heat transfer, pressure drop, wall temperature limits, and high-aspect-ratio channel tradeoffs.

Thermal Testing and Instrumentation

Worked with Type-K thermocouples, DAQ systems, thermal imaging, surface heat-flux testing, oxygen/pressure tracking, deformation timing, and test setup repeatability.

Simulation and Data Reduction

Used ANSYS transient thermal simulations with MATLAB/Python post-processing to compare thermal gradients, heating curves, oxygen depletion, and simulated trends against physical test results.

Manufacturing and DFM

Designed around FDM, machining, fixture fabrication, and metal DMP constraints including wall thickness, minimum feature size, powder removal, surface roughness, and inspection access.

Spacecraft Thermal Systems

Built trade studies for heaters, radiators, heat pipes, heat switches, insulation, coatings, redundancy, recovery logic, and verification plans for spacecraft and Mars rover thermal control.

PROJECT 01
Project 01 · Propulsion

Regeneratively Cooled Rocket Thrust Chamber

I worked on a regeneratively cooled LOX/RP-1 thrust-chamber, where the core challenge was reducing hot-gas-side wall temperature while controlling coolant pressure drop and keeping the channels manufacturable.

Problem

The throat sees the highest heat flux, so there I minimize the thermal resistance between the hot-gas wall and coolant. In lower-flux chamber regions the priority flips, reduce pressure drop while keeping wall temperature within limits. I treated channel design as a coupled thermal · fluid · structural · manufacturing problem, not just a heat-transfer one.

My Work

I sized cooling-channel geometry (width, height, count) across two stations, the throat and the chamber, by building a 1-D thermal-resistance network from the hot gas through the wall and into the coolant, then solving for the coolant-side heat-transfer coefficient and pressure drop.

The channel ribs behave like fins. Increasing channel height adds wetted area and improves heat transfer to the coolant — but only until fin efficiency, pressure drop, and manufacturing limits take over.
Key Equations
\( T_{wall} = R_{th}\,q + T_c \)wall temp ← flux × resistance
\( Re = \dfrac{\rho V D_h}{\mu} \)coolant flow regime
\( Nu = 0.023\,Re^{0.8}\,Pr^{0.4} \)Nusselt correlation
\( h_c = \dfrac{Nu\,k_c}{D_h} \)heat-transfer coefficient
\( D_h = \dfrac{4A}{P} \)non-circular channels
\( \Delta P \sim f\,\dfrac{L}{D_h}\,\dfrac{\rho V^2}{2} \)pressure-drop penalty
Tradeoffs
↑ velocity → ↑ Re → ↑ h ↑ velocity → ↑ ΔP high aspect ratio → more sidewall area …but harder to manufacture DMP min wall thickness feature size · powder removal
What I Learned

Optimal channel geometry isn't a single number, it's a balance that shifts station-to-station between cooling performance, pressure budget, and what the printer can actually build. Framing it as a constrained, multi-objective problem made those tradeoffs explicit instead of accidental.

PROJECT 02
Project 02 · Spacecraft Fire Safety

PMMA Flame Extinction in Microgravity

At the Berkeley Fire Lab I worked on research connected to NASA's SoFIE-MIST investigation aboard the ISS, studying how solid fuels ignite, spread flame, and extinguish under spacecraft-relevant oxygen, pressure, and flow conditions.

Problem

Compare PMMA flame extinction in Earth gravity versus microgravity. The key parameter is the limiting oxygen concentration (LOC), the oxygen level at which a flame extinguishes.

Experiment

Black PMMA cylinders burned in a sealed chamber. Earth gravity carried forced + buoyant flow; microgravity had forced flow only. Forced flow was 10 cm/s, comparable to low-speed cabin ventilation, opposing the flame-spread direction.

40 kPa60 kPa80 kPa100 kPa O₂ tracked at 1 Hzsealed-chamber depletion
Key Result

Flames in microgravity persist at oxygen concentrations ~3–4% lower than on Earth, so a flame that would self-extinguish on Earth can keep burning in space.

The implication: Earth-based flammability tests may not fully bound the spacecraft fire case. Without buoyancy, the transport of oxygen, heat, and pyrolysis gases changes, so ground tests don't always conservatively predict orbit.
Combustion Physics

Solid fuels don't burn directly, they must absorb heat, pyrolyze, and release gaseous fuel. Flame spread depends on whether heat feedback from the flame is enough to drive the next section of material to pyrolysis. Extinction is a competition between heat transfer and chemical kinetics; LOC occurs as flame-spread velocity → 0.

\( LOC = X_{O_2,\,\text{ext}} \)extinction oxygen fraction
\( q''_{conv} + q''_{cond} + q''_{rad} - q''_{re\text{-}rad} = 0 \)surface energy balance
\( q''_{conv} = h\,(T_f - T_p) \)flame → surface feedback
\( Da = \dfrac{t_{flow}}{t_{chem}} \)Damköhler: flow vs. chemistry
\( U_m \approx \sqrt{g\,\beta\,\Delta T\, l_c} + U_{forced} \)buoyant + forced flow
Spacecraft Relevance

For crewed vehicles, fire safety is a life-support and thermal-control issue, you can't open a window or rely on Earth-like buoyancy. Future cabins may run sub-atmospheric pressure and elevated oxygen to cut EVA prep time, which directly changes material flammability. This work informs safer cabin environments and material-screening standards.

PROJECT 03
Project 03 · Thermal Protection

Bio-Inspired FDM Composite Heat-Shield Tiles

I studied how FDM-printed, bio-inspired tile geometries affect thermal response, heat spreading, and deformation under high thermal loads, comparing material and geometry side by side.

Objective

Not to replace flight-grade TPS, but to study how geometry and material choice change heat spreading, deformation, and thermal resistance under controlled heating, and whether additive + bio-inspired geometry could enable lighter, lower-cost concepts.

Materials & Geometries
Nylon / PA6Carbon-fiber nylon / PA6-CF
Flat (baseline)HoneycombSpikesTessellated spikesScales
Simulation & Testing

ANSYS transient-thermal simulations, validated against physical heat-gun testing. I built a thermocouple-based DAQ system for real-time back-surface temperature, paired with thermal imaging to catch material failure thresholds and deformation onset.

\( q'' = h\,(T_\infty - T_s) \)convective load from heat gun
\( \alpha = \dfrac{k}{\rho\,c_p} \)thermal diffusivity
\( Bi = \dfrac{hL}{k} \quad ; \quad Bi < 0.1 \Rightarrow \text{lumped valid} \)PA6-CF lumped ✓ · nylon ✗
Key Results

Nylon (k ≈ 0.25 W/m·K) acted like an insulator and built large internal gradients; carbon-fiber nylon (k ≈ 25 W/m·K) spread heat far more evenly. The scale geometry gave the best deformation resistance. Spikes looked strong in simulation, acting like fins, but deformed fastest in real testing as protruding features concentrated heat and softened.

The sim-vs-test mismatch was the real lesson: layer lines, voids, anisotropy, surface roughness, emissivity effects, and polymer softening mean simulation finds trends, but hardware testing decides the answer.
Lessons Learned

Material sets how fast heat conducts; geometry sets where heat concentrates and how the structure deforms. Connecting ANSYS, DAQ-based testing, material properties, and manufacturability is what actually evaluates a thermal-hardware concept.

PROJECT 04
Project 04 · Systems Engineering

NASA L'SPACE Mars Rover Thermal Control System

For NASA L'SPACE I worked the thermal-control section of a Mars-rover concept, driving component selection, trade studies, redundancy, and verification planning under simulated Martian conditions.

Mission Thermal Problem

Keep internal components within safe operating limits while surviving the Martian environment: cold temperatures, internal electronics heat, UV / radiation, thermal cycling, all under limited mass, volume, and power, with no human repair. Requirement band ≈ −40 °C to 50 °C, with the ability to reject and generate ≥ 20 °C of swing.

Thermal Architecture

A hybrid passive + active system, no single point of thermal control:

Aerogel insulationPatch heatersPassive radiator Heat pipes / VCHPHeat switchesCoating / Kapton
Trade Study Criteria

Each subassembly was scored on weighted criteria, not performance alone, but mass / space, reliability & redundancy, technology readiness (TRL), functionality, and complexity.

\( Q_{rad} = \varepsilon\,\sigma\,A\,(T_s^4 - T_{env}^4) \)radiative rejection
\( q''_{solar} = \alpha\,G \)absorbed solar flux
\( P = VI = I^2R = \dfrac{V^2}{R} \)heater power budget
Redundancy & Recovery

I ran failure logic across the architecture so no single component loss ends the mission: if patch heaters fail, switches + insulation limit overcooling; if the radiator fails, heat pipes + switches redirect heat; if the VCHP fails, heaters + switches hold thermal balance. The goal was to design out single-point thermal failures.

Verification Plan

Every requirement mapped to a test, analysis, or inspection: temperature survival via thermal cycling (−40 °C to 50 °C), UV resistance via radiation exposure, coating performance via absorptivity / emissivity analysis, and regulation via heat-switch testing. That's requirements-driven engineering, traced end to end.

// Trade study — Insulation method (Aerogel selected, 81.5%)
// Trade study — Heaters (Patch heaters selected, 65%)
// Trade study — Heat switches (Differential-expansion selected, 70%)
// Trade study — Heat-pipe system (VCHP selected, 66%)
// Trade study — Radiators (Passive structure radiator selected, 85.5%)

Engineering Approach

Thermal hardware is never only a heat-transfer problem.

Across these projects I learned to start from first principles, identify the dominant heat-transfer mechanism, design or simulate the system, test the hardware, compare data to expectations, and iterate on what the results show. It's also a reliability, manufacturing, integration, and test problem — and I treat it that way.
